title: Biomass Recycling Strategies Affect Microbial Stability and Yeast Performance in Sugarcane Fermentation
content: Microbial stability is a major determinant of fermentation efficiency during repeated in-dustrial fermentations, yet the effects of biomass management on yeast physiology and microbial dynamics remain insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated two bio-mass management strategies—continuous biomass recycling and weekly biomass re-placement—for four commercial Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains during repeated sugarcane juice fermentations. Fermentation performance was assessed over ten consecutive cycles by monitoring fermentation time, yeast viability, viable cell population, lactic acid bacteria counts, metabolite production, and multivariate analysis. Biomass management affected microbial stability and fermentation performance. Weekly biomass replacement main-tained high yeast viability, limited bacterial proliferation, reduced organic acid accumula-tion, and resulted in more homogeneous fermentations. In contrast, continuous biomass recycling promoted progressive physiological deterioration, increased microbial contami-nation, and greater metabolic variability among cycles. DistilaMax CN exhibited the greatest physiological robustness, maintaining stable ethanol production, efficient sugar utilization, and high cell viability under both strategies. Principal component analysis demonstrated that fermentation performance was closely associated with microbial stabil-ity and strain-dependent physiological adaptation. These findings demonstrate that bio-mass management shapes microbial stability and strain-specific physiological responses during repeated sugarcane juice fermentations, providing a basis for improving the ro-bustness and consistency of industrial fermentation processes.
